newsitem.title: UK: Derivatives hassle EMU contract continuity - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Derivatives hassle EMU contract continuity - lawyer.

text.p: The OTC derivatives market may pose the main threat to the vexed problem of how to establish continuity of contract when the euro is introduced in 1999, a leading lawyer told delegates at a conference in London. "A loophole is most likely (to be found) in the derivatives market," said Geoffrey Yeowart, a partner at British law firm Lovell White Durrant and chairman of the single currency working party of the City of London Law Society.
Yeowart said a party might be able to walk away from a contract if it could prove to a court the contract had become, in legal terms, "frustrated".

"It will likely only affect a few cases. But that could unsettle financial markets until there is a court ruling," he said at a conference on the legal implications of European economic and monetary union, adding a final verdict could take years to reach.

The most obvious arguement for frustration was foreseeability -- whether both parties could have foreseen the introduction of the euro and its implications when they signed the contract, Yeowart said.
"EMU has been foreseeable since the signing of the Maastricht Treaty in 1993 and possibly earlier...but its effect may not have been clear," he said.

Other events that could frustrate a contract included the disappearance of pricing sources, indices and settlement systems with the advent of EMU, Yeowart said. "Long-term supply contracts are (often) based on currency exchange rates."

Nicholas O'Neill, legal counsel at the European Monetary Institute, reminded the conference that a regulation would be adopted under Article 235 of the European Union by early next year which would contain a provision on continuity of contracts.

"The EMI supports the idea of including a carefuly drafted provision on contractual continuity...it is vital for the financial markets that they have certainty on this issue as soon as possible," O'Neill said.

The regulation covering contractual continuity would also specify the euro as the name of the single currency, provide for one-to-one conversion from the Ecu and deal with rounding, likely to be to the first six significant figures, O'Neill said.

Article 235 is a sweep-up provision allowing the EU to agree unanimously on a measure for which provision was not expressly made in the Treaty but which is required to achieve one of the objectives of the Community. The Ecu was defined in a regulation adopted under Article 235.
Yeowart said: "Legislation can't cope with every eventuality but we must ensure a robust framework."
In any event whatever might happen in Europe will have little bearing on how courts elsewhere in the world act.

Niall Lenihan, at U.S. law firm Davis Polk & Wardwell, said there was a reasonable probability New York courts would throw out any action brought on the grounds of unforeseeability given that monetary union was one of the founding tenets of the EU.

"The tortuous Byzantine path (of accepting the unforeseeability argument) means U.S. courts are likely to view the euro as a commodity in the same way they see the mark or French franc as a commodity."
Lenihan said while there wasn't much recent case history, the U.S. court decision during its civil war to endorse the paper dollar's replacement of the gold dollar was pivotal.
Lenihan said the verdict meant that under U.S. law, contracts could be settled in whatever was the accepted unit of money at the time.
